desc:
A sorted array of distinct integers was cut at some position into a front part and a back part and the two parts were swapped, giving nums (a cut at the very start or end leaves it unchanged). For [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] one possible result is [5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 4].

Given nums and an integer x (which need not occur in the array), return how many elements of nums are strictly smaller than x. For nums = [5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 4] and x = 5 the answer is 4 (the values 0, 1, 2 and 4). Use O(log n) time.
constraints: nums is a rotation of a sorted array
hints: In a plain sorted array the answer is the 'insertion position' of x, found by binary search. What blocks that here?
Imagine reading the array circularly from its minimum. That virtual array is sorted, and position j of it is nums[(s + j) % n], where s is the index of the minimum.
Find s with one binary search, then run a second binary search for the first virtual position whose value is at least x; that position is the count.
editorial: The answer only depends on the multiset of values, not on where they sit. So count in the sorted view: find the first index j in sorted order with value ≥ x; exactly j elements are smaller.

Step 1 finds the start s of the sorted order (compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]; distinct values mean no ties). Step 2 is an ordinary lower-bound search over virtual indices 0..n-1, translating each index j to nums[(s + j) % n]. Both are O(log n) and need O(1) space.
